seo.title: Playwright Python Tutorial #20 — 12 real scenarios (drill room)
seo.description: Twelve situations you will actually meet: the moving table row, the invisible iframe field, the runaway tab, the 25-minute suite, the 3am CI failure. Scenario, four options, then the answer.

scenes.narration: Nineteen lessons behind you. So: twelve real situations, and one question — what would you actually do?

Welcome back to THE NBX STUDIO, and welcome to the Drill Room. Nothing new gets taught in this one. Everything here you have already been shown, which is exactly why it is worth finding out whether you can reach for it under pressure.

Here's how each one runs. You get the situation, four options, then a few seconds of quiet to commit before I say anything. Say it out loud if you can, because a guess you've said out loud is one you'll remember getting right.

ruleTest.rule: situation · four options · commit · then the answer
ruleTest.caption: pause any time you want longer

scenes.narration: Level one first, and these three are the ones that separate somebody who has read the docs from somebody who has actually written a test.

First one. A signup form's Work email field, and the input's got an auto-generated id, a class, and a placeholder. Which locator first? Ready? Option B — get by label, because that id changes the moment anyone edits the form.

quiz.question: Which locator do you reach for first?
quiz.why: That id is auto-generated. It will change and your test will not.

scenes.narration: That's the ladder from episode four, ordered by how likely a locator is to survive somebody else's redesign. A label is what a human reads, so a label is what you reach for. An auto-generated id is a number a framework invented this morning.

pyramid.headline: Robots Love Pizza, Tacos, Two Cokes

scenes.narration: Number two. Your test clicks Save, then asserts the Saved toast is visible. Passes locally, fails in CI weekly. The professional fix? Ready? Go with B. expect retries, so the toast gets five seconds to turn up.

quiz.question: Passes locally, fails in CI weekly. Fix?

options.text: Re-run CI until it goes green
Pay for a bigger CI machine

quiz.why: expect() retries for five seconds, and passes the instant it appears.

scenes.narration: And notice that expect is not just more reliable than a sleep, expect is usually faster. A sleep of three seconds costs you three seconds even on a good day. expect passes the moment that toast lands, which is often under a hundred milliseconds.

ruleTest.rule: expect() is more reliable AND usually faster than sleep
ruleTest.caption: a sleep costs you the full three seconds

scenes.narration: Here's a nasty one. A city box shows suggestions as you type. You call fill with Chennai, the value lands, and the dropdown never opens. Why? Ready? The answer's B — press sequentially, because fill never fires a single keystroke.

quiz.question: fill() sets the value but no dropdown. Why?

options.text: The site has a bug to report

quiz.why: fill() sets the value in one shot, so no key events ever fire.

scenes.narration: This one catches everybody once. fill sets the value in a single shot, so the page never sees a keystroke, and an autocomplete listening for keystrokes has nothing to hear. press sequentially types like a person, so the dropdown wakes up.

codeRun.caption: one sets a value. one types.

lines.detail: the value lands in one shot
lines.label: silent

lines.detail: typed key by key, like a person
lines.label: typed

scenes.narration: Level two now. These four are the ones that get asked in interviews, and the ones that cost people an afternoon when they meet them for the first time.

chapter.title: Level two
chapter.subtitle: the ones that cost an afternoon

scenes.narration: Level two, and this one's an interview favourite. Thirty users in a table, and you must deactivate only Morpheus, whose row keeps moving. What's robust? Ready? C is the one. Filter the rows by text, then act inside the match.

quiz.question: Deactivate one user whose row keeps moving?

options.text: Loop rows with an if inside

quiz.why: Locate all rows, filter by content, then act INSIDE the match.

scenes.narration: That's the filter recipe from episode ten, and the important half is the last step. Locate every row, narrow to the one containing Morpheus, then press the button inside that row — not the twelfth button on the page, which belongs to whoever's sitting there today.

rowFilter.caption: narrow to the row. act inside it.

scenes.narration: Now this one wastes afternoons. The card number field in a Stripe widget is right there on screen, you can see it, and fill times out anyway. What's happening? Ready? C. That field is sitting inside an iframe.

quiz.question: You can SEE the field. fill() times out. Why?
quiz.why: "I can see it but Playwright cannot find it" is the iframe symptom.

scenes.narration: Learn that symptom by heart, because it saves an hour every time. I can see it and Playwright can't find it means a document inside a document, and payment widgets are always iframes. Frame locator steps inside, and the same locator works fine.

frameBoundary.caption: you can see it. the page cannot reach it.

scenes.narration: Next. Clicking View invoice opens a new tab, and your title assertion fails, because page still points at the tab you started on. The fix? Ready? B — expect popup, armed before the click, because a listener can't catch what already happened.

quiz.question: A click opens a new tab. Assertion fails. Fix?

options.text: Sleep, then check the title again
Ask the devs to stop using tabs

quiz.why: Arm the listener BEFORE the click, then read info.value.

scenes.narration: Trap, then trigger. The order is the entire answer here, because a listener armed after the event has already happened catches precisely nothing. So you arm expect popup first, you do the click inside that block, and afterwards info dot value is the new page.

trapTrigger.caption: arm it first. then cause the event.

scenes.narration: Try this one. Upload avatar opens an operating system file picker, and your locators can't touch an OS window. So what's the Playwright way? Ready? You want B. Hand the file straight to the input and skip the dialog entirely.

quiz.question: An OS file picker opens. Locators cannot reach it.

options.text: Drag and drop with mouse events

quiz.why: Hand the file straight to the <input type="file"> and skip the dialog.

scenes.narration: You never open that picker at all, which is the bit that feels like cheating. Set input files hands the file directly to the file input underneath, exactly as if a person had chosen it, and the operating system window never gets involved.

pickerBypass.caption: skip the dialog. hand it the file.

scenes.narration: And level three. These five are the senior calls — the ones where the right answer is not a different line of code, but a different idea about where the test should even happen.

Level three now. Your product manager wants the orders page for a user with zero orders, and staging hasn't got one. How do you test that today? Ready? B again — mock the response, because impossible data is one line.

quiz.question: You need a user with ZERO orders. None exists.

options.text: route() and fulfill an empty list

quiz.why: route + fulfill makes impossible data one line of code.

scenes.narration: The empty state is the one everybody ships without ever looking at, because producing it for real is somebody else's ticket. Mock the response and the impossible state becomes one line, available on every single run, for ever.

A hundred and eighty tests, twenty five minutes, and every one logs in through the interface at six seconds a go. Get it under ten. Which combination? Ready? C. Storage state, then dash n auto, because those two stack.

quiz.question: 180 tests, 25 minutes. Get under 10.

options.text: A bigger CI machine, that is all
Convert every test to an API test

quiz.why: One real login instead of 180, then split what is left across workers.

scenes.narration: Two ideas stacked, and the order matters. Storage state removes a hundred and seventy nine logins, which is roughly eighteen minutes gone on its own. Then dash n auto takes whatever is left and spreads it across workers, because the work never got faster — the work just stopped queuing.

workerSpread.caption: log in once. then spread the rest.

scenes.narration: Here's one you'll actually hit. The app should show a Retry button when the products API returns a five hundred, and the real API won't fail on demand. Test it permanently? Ready? B — route the call and fulfil a five hundred yourself.

quiz.question: Test the 500 screen. The API never fails.
quiz.why: fulfill(status=500) fakes the disaster reliably, in milliseconds.

scenes.narration: Route puts you in the mail room, and once you are standing in the mail room every request stops at your desk on the way past. You decide what happens to each one. Answer it yourself with a five hundred, and the disaster you could never schedule happens on cue, every run.

mailRoom.caption: every letter stops at your desk

scenes.narration: The three a.m. mystery. test checkout fails in CI weekly, always passes on your machine, and the log just says TimeoutError. How do you see what happened? Ready? B. Keep a trace, because a log can't show you the page.

quiz.question: Fails weekly in CI. Never locally. Log says timeout.

options.text: Keep a trace, then show-trace it
Blame the network and move on

quiz.why: The trace is a flight recorder from the actual failing run.

scenes.narration: A trace is a flight recorder, and that is not a metaphor I am stretching. You get a DOM snapshot before and after every action, the console, and the network — recorded on the machine where the failure actually happened, which is a machine that no longer exists.

traceScrub.caption: the failing run, kept in a file

scenes.narration: Last one, and it separates levels. Archiving a project needs a project, and building one through the interface is twelve clicks. How does a senior structure that? Ready? B — create it by API, because the create form isn't what you're testing.

quiz.question: The setup is 12 clicks. The test is one click.

options.text: Do the twelve clicks each run
Create by API, archive in the UI

quiz.why: UI for the behaviour under test, API for the scenery.

scenes.narration: Nobody is testing the create form today, so the create form is scenery. One post request builds the project in about a tenth of a second, and then the browser opens for the one thing you actually came to check. When that test goes red, you know why, because the only interface in it is the archive flow.

stageHandoff.verdict: when it fails, you know why
stageHandoff.caption: scenery by phone. the scene on stage.

scenes.narration: If you got most of those, you are genuinely ready for an interview, and more importantly you are ready for a Tuesday. Notice how few of the answers were a clever line of code. Nearly all of them were a decision about where the test should happen at all.

points.text: API for scenery, UI for behaviour

scenes.narration: One episode left, and it is the cheat sheet — every command, on one screen, for the night before an interview. The whole course is free, over at the Playwright Dojo.
